questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning?
options: They are three completely separate fields
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI
AI is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of deep learning
Machine learning and deep learning are synonyms for AI
questions.explanation: AI is the broadest field, machine learning is a subset of AI focused on learning from data, and deep learning is a subset of ML using multi-layered neural networks.

questions.question: What is a perceptron?
options: A database for storing neural network weights
A type of decision tree algorithm
The simplest form of an artificial neuron that computes a weighted sum and applies a threshold
A clustering algorithm for unlabeled data
questions.explanation: The perceptron, introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in 1957, is the simplest neural unit: it sums weighted inputs, adds a bias, and outputs a result based on a threshold function.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an activation function in a neural network?
options: To introduce non-linearity so the network can learn complex patterns
To normalize the input data to a fixed range
To store learned parameters between training runs
To split the dataset into batches
questions.explanation: Without non-linear activation functions, stacking layers would be equivalent to a single linear transformation, limiting what the network can learn.

questions.question: Which activation function squashes its output to a range between 0 and 1, making it useful for probabilities?
options: ReLU
Tanh
Sigmoid
Softmax only
questions.explanation: The sigmoid function maps any real number to the interval (0, 1), which is why it is often used on output layers for binary classification.

questions.question: What does backpropagation do in neural network training?
options: It shuffles the training data between epochs
It propagates input data forward through all layers
It removes neurons that contribute little to predictions
It computes gradients of the loss with respect to each weight so they can be updated
questions.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute how much each weight contributed to the error, enabling gradient-based weight updates.

questions.question: What is the difference between training and inference?
options: Training adjusts model weights using data; inference uses the trained model to make predictions
Training happens on GPUs; inference happens on CPUs only
Training is unsupervised; inference is supervised
There is no difference; they are two names for the same phase
questions.explanation: During training the model learns parameters from data. Inference is the deployment phase where the frozen model makes predictions on new inputs.

questions.question: A model achieves 99% accuracy on training data but only 62% on unseen data. What is this called?
options: Underfitting
Overfitting
Convergence
Regularization
questions.explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training data including its noise, so it fails to generalize to new examples.

questions.question: Which scenario describes underfitting?
options: The model performs well on training data but poorly on test data
The model performs poorly on both training and test data
The model performs equally well on all data
The model only works with small datasets
questions.explanation: Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns, so it performs poorly everywhere.

questions.question: Which technique helps prevent overfitting by randomly disabling a fraction of neurons during each training step?
options: Data augmentation
Gradient clipping
Dropout
Batch normalization
questions.explanation: Dropout randomly sets some neuron outputs to zero during training, forcing the network to learn redundant, more robust representations.

questions.question: What does the Turing Test, proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, evaluate?
options: Whether a computer can outperform humans at chess
Whether a machine's conversational responses are indistinguishable from a human's
Whether a neural network can pass graduate-level exams
Whether an algorithm runs in polynomial time
questions.explanation: In the Turing Test, an interrogator converses with hidden entities; if the machine cannot reliably be distinguished from a human, it is said to exhibit intelligent behavior.

questions.question: Who invented the perceptron in 1957, an early milestone in neural network history?
options: Frank Rosenblatt
Alan Turing
Geoffrey Hinton
John McCarthy
questions.explanation: Frank Rosenblatt developed the perceptron at Cornell in 1957, marking the first practical learning algorithm for artificial neurons.

questions.question: Why is AlexNet (2012) considered a landmark in AI history?
options: It was the first neural network ever built
It defeated the world chess champion
It passed the Turing Test for the first time
Its deep convolutional network won ImageNet by a large margin, sparking the deep learning boom
questions.explanation: AlexNet's dominant ImageNet victory in 2012 demonstrated the power of deep CNNs trained on GPUs and triggered widespread adoption of deep learning.

questions.question: The transformer architecture that powers modern large language models is primarily built around which mechanism?
options: Convolution
Recurrence
Attention
Decision trees
questions.explanation: Transformers replace recurrence with self-attention, allowing each token to directly weigh the relevance of every other token in the sequence.

questions.question: In a transformer, what does the attention mechanism compute?
options: How much focus each token should place on every other token in the sequence
The physical memory address of each embedding
The number of layers needed for a task
The gradient of the loss function
questions.explanation: Attention produces weighted combinations of value vectors, where the weights reflect how relevant each input token is to the token currently being processed.

questions.question: What is a large language model (LLM) fundamentally trained to do?
options: Classify images into categories
Predict the next token in a sequence of text
Store encyclopedias in a lookup table
Translate only between two specific languages
questions.explanation: LLMs are trained with a next-token prediction objective over massive text corpora, which gives rise to broad language understanding and generation abilities.

questions.question: In the context of language models, what is a token?
options: A security key for accessing the model
A reward signal used in reinforcement learning
A chunk of text such as a word, subword, or character that the model processes
A unit of GPU memory
questions.explanation: Text is broken into tokens (often subword units) before processing; model context limits and pricing are typically measured in tokens.

questions.question: What is an epoch in machine learning training?
options: A single weight update
One complete pass through the entire training dataset
The time it takes to train a model
A historical era of AI research
questions.explanation: One epoch means every training example has been seen once; models usually train for many epochs with weights updated each batch.

questions.question: What does a loss function measure during training?
options: How fast the model runs
How much memory the model uses
The size of the training dataset
The difference between the model's predictions and the true targets
questions.explanation: The loss function quantifies prediction error, providing the signal that gradient descent uses to improve the model.

questions.question: Which optimization algorithm iteratively updates weights in the direction that most reduces the loss?
options: K-means
Gradient descent
Binary search
Principal component analysis
questions.explanation: Gradient descent moves parameters opposite the gradient of the loss, taking steps proportional to the learning rate toward a minimum.

questions.question: Which type of neural network is specifically designed to exploit spatial structure, making it the classic choice for image tasks?
options: Convolutional neural network (CNN)
Recurrent neural network (RNN)
Radial basis function network
Hopfield network
questions.explanation: CNNs use shared convolutional filters that detect local patterns like edges and textures, which suits grid-structured data such as images.

questions.question: Which neural network family was classically used for sequential data like text or time series before transformers became dominant?
options: Convolutional neural networks
Generative adversarial networks
Autoencoders
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs, including LSTMs)
questions.explanation: RNNs process sequences step by step while maintaining a hidden state; gated variants like LSTM and GRU were designed to capture longer dependencies.

questions.question: What distinguishes generative AI from discriminative models?
options: Generative AI can create new content such as text, images, or audio
Generative AI only works on numerical data
Discriminative models always require more data
There is no difference between the two
questions.explanation: Generative models learn the distribution of the data so they can produce new samples, whereas discriminative models learn to distinguish between categories.

questions.question: A hiring model trained mostly on résumés from male applicants starts rejecting qualified female candidates. Which AI ethics issue does this illustrate?
options: Hallucination
Model bias inherited from biased training data
Overfitting
Vanishing gradients
questions.explanation: Models learn patterns from their training data; if the data encodes historical bias, the model can reproduce or amplify unfair outcomes.

questions.question: In LLMs, what is a hallucination?
options: A crash caused by too many tokens
A debugging mode of the transformer
Confidently generated output that is factually false or unsupported
An unusually slow inference pass
questions.explanation: LLMs can produce plausible-sounding but incorrect statements because they generate statistically likely text rather than verified facts.

questions.question: Learning rate, number of layers, and batch size are examples of what?
options: Hyperparameters chosen before training
Weights learned during training
Activation functions
Loss values
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters are configuration choices set before training begins, unlike weights and biases which are learned from data.

questions.question: What are the learned values inside a neural network that get adjusted during training called?
options: Hyperparameters
Tokens
Weights (parameters) and biases
Features
questions.explanation: Weights and biases are the trainable parameters updated by gradient descent; their count defines the model's size.

questions.question: A fully connected layer receives 16 inputs and produces 10 outputs, with one bias per neuron. How many trainable parameters does it contain?
questions.explanation: Weights = 16 x 10 = 160, plus 10 biases = 170 parameters.

questions.question: A dataset of 12,800 samples is trained with a batch size of 64. How many optimizer steps (weight updates) occur in one epoch?
questions.explanation: Steps per epoch = 12,800 / 64 = 200.

questions.question: A 28x28 input image passes through a 3x3 convolution with stride 1 and no padding. What is the spatial size of the output feature map?
questions.explanation: Output size = 28 - 3 + 1 = 26, so the feature map is 26x26.

questions.question: Why do transformers add positional encodings to token embeddings?
options: To prevent vanishing gradients during backpropagation
Because self-attention is permutation-invariant and cannot distinguish token order on its own
To compress embeddings into fewer dimensions
To normalize embedding magnitudes to unit length
questions.explanation: Self-attention treats input as a set with no inherent ordering, so positional encodings inject sequence order information.

questions.question: What does a dropout layer do during inference (prediction)?
options: Randomly drops neurons with the same probability as in training
Multiplies activations by a random noise term
Remains fully active; dropout applies only during training, with activations rescaled
Permanently removes the weakest neurons from the model
questions.explanation: At inference all neurons stay active; dropout is a training-time regularizer, and outputs are scaled so expectations match.
